statements.notes: Hypotheses are exactly the target's: [T1Space M] [SecondCountableTopology M], C.IsCauchySurfaceOn W S, C.CausallyArcConnectedOn W, antisymmetry of C.le W in the shape of Ers482Solution's hcaus (Causal/Ers482Solution.lean:250), C.PastInextensible W I σ, ∃ t ∈ I, σ t ∈ C.Jplus W S. Conclusion ∃ t ∈ I, σ t ∈ S. There is no TailFree hypothesis, which the #check output in axioms.txt and my own run confirm. Every notion is the library's own: PastInextensible (Causal/Inextensible.lean:322, DEC-13), IsCauchySurfaceOn (Causal/Cauchy.lean:73, DEC-14), Jplus (Causal/Causality.lean:92), CausallyArcConnectedOn (Causal/ArcConnected.lean:127). The file defines nothing new. Against Sbierski (sbierski2023c.txt:356–358, :1139–1144) the Lean is at least the paper's step: the given point may be any point of the curve (his 'starts in' and 'to the future it contains a point'), it may lie in J⁺ (which contains I⁺), and W is any open set (M is W = ⊤). Sbierski's Lorentzian 'past inextendible' (no past endpoint) implies DEC-13 past-inextensibility, by continuity of c' at inf φ(I). So the hypothesis a consumer must supply is implied by his, and the DEC-13 reading is the library's standing one (DEC-11/13). It is recorded as a REPORT question and is not decided here.

checks.findings_of_the_report: Neither sharpness construction is a claim that the paper is wrong. Both are hedged ('look necessary', 'not checked in Lean') and both hold up. In the ray-plus-circle example ≤ is total on the circle, S = {y} meets every maximal curve as a set, the ray over ]-∞,0] is past-inextensible, q ∈ J⁺({y}), and the ray misses y. In the two lines with (s,0) ≤ (r,1) for s ≤ 0 ≤ r+1, the relation is antisymmetric and transitive, (0,0) ≤ (-1,1), and t ↦ (t,1) over ]-∞,-1] misses (0,1). The example also shows that S is not acausal there, which is the step arc-connectedness supplies. The finding that 'deliverable (1) is already exists_subArc_of_tailFree' is true: its conclusion is exactly the extension form the target asks for.

In a model where curves are continuous, Sbierski's 'no past endpoint' already implies it: a past extension c' over I' with a parameter below the final segment φ(I) puts inf φ(I) in I', so c'(inf φ(I)) would be a past endpoint of σ.
